title: DNA Builder: Base Pair Match
description: Match nucleotide bases to build DNA strands! Swap adjacent bases on the grid to create chains of Adenine, Thymine, Cytosine, Guanine, and RNA Uracil. Learn about genetics, DNA structure, and the base pairing rules that make life possible through engaging puzzle gameplay.
learning_objectives: Understand the four DNA bases and their pairing rules (A-T, C-G)
Learn the structure of the DNA double helix and how it encodes information
Discover the difference between DNA and RNA nucleotides
Practice pattern recognition through strategic base pair matching
Build foundational genetics knowledge through interactive gameplay
Explore how mutations occur when base pairs are mismatched
how_to_play: Swap two adjacent nucleotide base tiles to create a match of 3 or more identical bases in a row or column.
Matched bases bond together and clear from the grid, earning you helix points.
Cleared tiles cascade down and new bases fill in from the top — chain reactions build longer DNA strands!
Longer matches (4 or 5 in a row) earn bonus points and trigger powerful genetic cascades.
You have 25 moves to reach the target score of 500 helix points.
Remember: in real DNA, Adenine pairs with Thymine, and Cytosine pairs with Guanine!

storybook_pages.title: Inside the Cell
storybook_pages.text: Zoom into the nucleus of a cell and discover the blueprint of life — DNA! Nucleotide bases are floating freely, waiting to be matched into the elegant double helix structure. Your task: arrange the bases by matching identical ones to build functioning DNA strands.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: inside a cell nucleus with a DNA double helix partially built, colorful nucleotide base tiles (A, T, C, G) floating on a puzzle grid, microscope frame around the scene, scientific cartoon style

storybook_pages.title: The Base Pair Rules
storybook_pages.text: In real DNA, Adenine (A) always pairs with Thymine (T), and Cytosine (C) always pairs with Guanine (G). RNA uses Uracil (U) instead of Thymine. Match three or more identical bases to score — but remember these pairing rules for bonus knowledge!
storybook_pages.image_prompt: four DNA base characters holding hands in pairs: red A with blue T, green C with yellow G, plus a purple U (RNA) standing nearby, educational diagram with arrows showing pairing rules, cartoon biology style

storybook_pages.title: Genome Complete
storybook_pages.text: You've matched enough bases to build a complete DNA strand! Every match taught you about the fundamental code that makes all living things unique. From eye color to disease resistance, DNA holds the secrets of life — and now you understand how it works.
storybook_pages.image_prompt: beautiful completed DNA double helix spiraling upward, glowing with all four base pair colors, a trophy shaped like a chromosome, scientific celebration with confetti-like nucleotides, inspiring cartoon biology style

glossary_terms.definition: The process of selecting among alternatives based on available information and values.
glossary_terms.example: Choosing between two career paths based on income, passion, and long-term growth.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Good decision-making combines rational analysis with awareness of cognitive biases that distort judgment.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Leaders make high-stakes decisions daily — the quality of their process matters as much as the decision itself.

glossary_terms.definition: Analyzing information objectively to form a well-reasoned judgment.
glossary_terms.example: Questioning whether a statistic is representative before using it to make a decision.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Critical thinking involves identifying assumptions, evaluating evidence, and considering alternative perspectives.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Journalists fact-check before publishing; scientists replicate experiments before claiming discoveries.

glossary_terms.definition: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort and learning from failure.
glossary_terms.example: Seeing a poor game result as feedback on what to practice, not evidence of being bad at the game.
glossary_terms.deep_dive: Research by Carol Dweck shows people with growth mindsets achieve more and recover better from setbacks.
glossary_terms.real_world_example: Students who believe intelligence is fixed give up when challenged; those with growth mindset persist and improve.
